knowledge_point.title: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient

question.:question/problem:
Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
&\left(2 - z\right)^{2}\\
&{}-\left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}+2 x^{2}\\
&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

at $P(-1,1,1)$. Use $t\in\mathbb R$, with $t=0$ at $P$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring the variable terms together and set

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F(x,y,z)&=\left(2 - z\right)^{2}\\
&{}-\left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}+2 x^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=0$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others fixed. Use the product and chain rules, including signs from inner linear functions:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(x,y,z)&=4 x
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=-2 \left(2 - z\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=1\\
x&=-1\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=3
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=4 \left(-1\right)\\
&=-4
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=-1\\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=-2 \left(1\right)\\
&=-2
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(-1,1,1)=\langle -4,-1,-2\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $2$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=2\langle -4,-1,-2\rangle=\langle -8,-2,-4\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle -1,1,1\rangle+t\,\langle -8,-2,-4\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find a symmetric Cartesian equation of the normal line to the surface

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
&\left(y + 2\right)^{2}\\
&{}-\left(2 - z\right)\\
&{}+e^{\left(2 - z\right) x}\\
&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

at $P(0,-1,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring the variable terms together and set

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F(x,y,z)&=\left(y + 2\right)^{2}\\
&{}-\left(2 - z\right)\\
&{}+e^{\left(2 - z\right) x}
\end{aligned}
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=1$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others fixed. Use the product and chain rules, including signs from inner linear functions:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(x,y,z)&=\left(2 - z\right) e^{\left(2 - z\right) x}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=2 \left(y + 2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=1\\
&{}-x e^{\left(2 - z\right) x}
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=1\\
x&=0\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=\left(1\right) e^{\left(1\right) \left(0\right)}\\
&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=2 \left(1\right)\\
&=2
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=1\\
&{}-\left(0\right) e^{\left(1\right) \left(0\right)}\\
&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(0,-1,1)=\langle 1,2,1\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $-1$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=-1\langle 1,2,1\rangle=\langle -1,-2,-1\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle 0,-1,1\rangle+t\,\langle -1,-2,-1\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

The coordinate equations are

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
x&=- t\\
y&=- 2 t - 1\\
z&=1 - t
\end{aligned}
$$

Solve each for $t$ and equate the ratios:

$$
\frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y + 1}{-2}=\frac{z - 1}{-1}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find a symmetric Cartesian equation of the normal line to the surface

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
&\left(2 - z\right)^{2} x \left(y + 2\right)\\
&=-4
\end{aligned}
$$

at $P(-1,-1,0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring the variable terms together and set

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F(x,y,z)&=\left(2 - z\right)^{2} x \left(y + 2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=-4$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others fixed. Use the product and chain rules, including signs from inner linear functions:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(x,y,z)&=\left(2 - z\right)^{2} \left(y + 2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=\left(2 - z\right)^{2} x
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=-2 \left(2 - z\right) x \left(y + 2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=2\\
x&=-1\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=\left(2\right)^{2} \left(1\right)\\
&=4
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=\left(2\right)^{2} \left(-1\right)\\
&=-4
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=-2 \left(2\right) \left(-1\right) \left(1\right)\\
&=4
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(-1,-1,0)=\langle 4,-4,4\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $-1$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=-1\langle 4,-4,4\rangle=\langle -4,4,-4\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle -1,-1,0\rangle+t\,\langle -4,4,-4\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

The coordinate equations are

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
x&=- 4 t - 1\\
y&=4 t - 1\\
z&=- 4 t
\end{aligned}
$$

Solve each for $t$ and equate the ratios:

$$
\frac{x + 1}{-4}=\frac{y + 1}{4}=\frac{z}{-4}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find a symmetric Cartesian equation of the normal line to the surface

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
&-2 \left(2 - z\right) x \left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}+e^{\left(2 - z\right) + x + \left(y + 2\right)}\\
&=-3
\end{aligned}
$$

at $P(-1,-3,0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring the variable terms together and set

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F(x,y,z)&=-2 \left(2 - z\right) x \left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}+e^{\left(2 - z\right) + x + \left(y + 2\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=-3$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others fixed. Use the product and chain rules, including signs from inner linear functions:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(x,y,z)&=-2 \left(2 - z\right) \left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}+e^{\left(2 - z\right) + x + \left(y + 2\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=-2 \left(2 - z\right) x\\
&{}+e^{\left(2 - z\right) + x + \left(y + 2\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=-e^{\left(2 - z\right) + x + \left(y + 2\right)}\\
&{}+2 x \left(y + 2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=2\\
x&=-1\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=-2 \left(2\right) \left(-1\right)\\
&{}+e^{\left(2\right) + \left(-1\right) + \left(-1\right)}\\
&=5
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=-2 \left(2\right) \left(-1\right)\\
&{}+e^{\left(2\right) + \left(-1\right) + \left(-1\right)}\\
&=5
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=-e^{\left(2\right) + \left(-1\right) + \left(-1\right)}\\
&{}+2 \left(-1\right) \left(-1\right)\\
&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(-1,-3,0)=\langle 5,5,1\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $-1$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=-1\langle 5,5,1\rangle=\langle -5,-5,-1\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle -1,-3,0\rangle+t\,\langle -5,-5,-1\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

The coordinate equations are

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
x&=- 5 t - 1\\
y&=- 5 t - 3\\
z&=- t
\end{aligned}
$$

Solve each for $t$ and equate the ratios:

$$
\frac{x + 1}{-5}=\frac{y + 3}{-5}=\frac{z}{-1}.
$$

\end{aligned}

\small\begin{aligned}
x&=2 - 4 t\\
y&=2 t - 1\\
z&=- t - 1
\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{x - 2}{-4}=\frac{y + 1}{2}=\frac{z + 1}{-1}.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring the variable terms together and set

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F(x,y,z)&=-\left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}+\ln{\left(2 \left(2 - z\right) + x \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=0$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others fixed. Use the product and chain rules, including signs from inner linear functions:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(x,y,z)&=\frac{1}{2 \left(2 - z\right) + x}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=-\frac{2}{2 \left(2 - z\right) + x}
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=1\\
x&=-1\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=\frac{1}{2 \left(1\right) + \left(-1\right)}\\
&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=-1\\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=-\frac{2}{2 \left(1\right) + \left(-1\right)}\\
&=-2
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(-1,-2,1)=\langle 1,-1,-2\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $-1$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=-1\langle 1,-1,-2\rangle=\langle -1,1,2\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle -1,-2,1\rangle+t\,\langle -1,1,2\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

The coordinate equations are

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
x&=- t - 1\\
y&=t - 2\\
z&=2 t + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Solve each for $t$ and equate the ratios:

$$
\frac{x + 1}{-1}=\frac{y + 2}{1}=\frac{z - 1}{2}.
$$

$$

F(x,y,z)&=x^{2}\\
&{}-\left(y + 2\right)\\

\end{aligned}
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=0$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others fixed. Use the product and chain rules, including signs from inner linear functions:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(x,y,z)&=2 x\\
&{}+\left(2 - z\right) \cos{\left(\left(2 - z\right) x \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=-x \cos{\left(\left(2 - z\right) x \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=0\\
x&=-1\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=2 \left(-1\right)\\
&{}+\left(0\right) \cos{\left(\left(0\right) \left(-1\right) \right)}\\
&=-2
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=-1\\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=-\left(-1\right) \cos{\left(\left(0\right) \left(-1\right) \right)}\\
&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(-1,-1,2)=\langle -2,-1,1\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $-1$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=-1\langle -2,-1,1\rangle=\langle 2,1,-1\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle -1,-1,2\rangle+t\,\langle 2,1,-1\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

The coordinate equations are

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
x&=2 t - 1\\
y&=t - 1\\
z&=2 - t
\end{aligned}
$$

Solve each for $t$ and equate the ratios:

$$
\frac{x + 1}{2}=\frac{y + 1}{1}=\frac{z - 2}{-1}.

\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=-x\\
&{}-2 \left(2 - z\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=1\\
x&=-1\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=2
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=\left(1\right)\\
&{}+4 \left(-1\right)\\
&=-3
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=-1\\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=-\left(-1\right)\\
&{}-2 \left(1\right)\\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(-1,0,1)=\langle -3,-1,-1\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $2$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=2\langle -3,-1,-1\rangle=\langle -6,-2,-2\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle -1,0,1\rangle+t\,\langle -6,-2,-2\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
&\left(y + 2\right)^{2} \sin{\left(\left(2 - z\right)^{2} x \right)}\\
&=x\\
&{}-\frac{\pi}{2}\\
&{}+\left(2 - z\right)^{2} \left(y + 2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

at $P(\frac{\pi}{2},-1,3)$. Use $t\in\mathbb R$, with $t=0$ at $P$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring the variable terms together and set

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F(x,y,z)&=-x\\
&{}+\left(y + 2\right)^{2} \sin{\left(\left(2 - z\right)^{2} x \right)}\\
&{}-\left(2 - z\right)^{2} \left(y + 2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=- \frac{\pi}{2}$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others fixed. Use the product and chain rules, including signs from inner linear functions:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(x,y,z)&=-1\\
&{}+\left(2 - z\right)^{2} \left(y + 2\right)^{2} \cos{\left(\left(2 - z\right)^{2} x \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=-\left(2 - z\right)^{2}\\
&{}+2 \left(y + 2\right) \sin{\left(\left(2 - z\right)^{2} x \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=2 \left(2 - z\right) \left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}-2 \left(2 - z\right) x \left(y + 2\right)^{2} \cos{\left(\left(2 - z\right)^{2} x \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=-1\\
x&=\frac{\pi}{2}\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=-1\\
&{}+\left(-1\right)^{2} \left(1\right)^{2} \cos{\left(\left(-1\right)^{2} \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)}\\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=-\left(-1\right)^{2}\\
&{}+2 \left(1\right) \sin{\left(\left(-1\right)^{2} \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)}\\
&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=2 \left(-1\right) \left(1\right)\\
&{}-2 \left(-1\right) \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \left(1\right)^{2} \cos{\left(\left(-1\right)^{2} \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)}\\
&=-2
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(\frac{\pi}{2},-1,3)=\langle -1,1,-2\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $2$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=2\langle -1,1,-2\rangle=\langle -2,2,-4\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle \frac{\pi}{2},-1,3\rangle+t\,\langle -2,2,-4\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$
